kurals.tamil:
இற்பிறந்தார் கண்அல்லது இல்லை இயல்பாகச்
செப்பமும் நாணும் ஒருங்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Irpirandhaar kan alladhu illai iyalpaagach
cheppamum naanum orungu.
kurals.meaning: Rectitude and a sense of shame, found together and as second nature, are seen only in those born into a good family.
kurals.elementary: Some children say sorry and play fair without anyone telling them, because they have seen it at home every day. Valluvar says that fairness and feeling bad about doing wrong come most naturally to people who grew up in a good home.
kurals.university: The chapter opens the Kudiyiyal (குடியியல், the section on the citizen and his family) of Porutpal, and its first couplet sets the theme: kudimai (குடிமை) is the character that a good lineage (இல், 'house', hence family) is expected to carry. Cheppam (செப்பம்) is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar as நடுவு நிலைமை, 'impartiality, rectitude', and by Solomon Pappaiah as purity of mind, word and deed; naanum (நாணும்) is shame or modesty, the recoil from what is unworthy. The force lies in iyalpaaga (இயல்பாக, 'by nature') and orungu (ஒருங்கு, 'together'): others may show one quality by effort, but the high-born show both effortlessly. Kalaignar's modern gloss reverses the direction, saying that only those who possess these qualities may be counted high-born, an egalitarian reading of a couplet that the medieval commentarial tradition read more literally. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna lists the qualities of one born to the divine nature (daivi sampad), among them truthfulness, freedom from anger, modesty (hri), steadiness, and freedom from pride, and says these belong to those so born.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita treats a cluster of virtues, including modesty, as the natural endowment of a certain kind of birth.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it speaks of shame and rectitude as an inborn inheritance rather than a learned skill.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the Gita's 'birth' is to a divine nature rather than to a human family, so the parallel is partial.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good; and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is evil: for of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that conduct flows naturally from the inner store a person carries.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's iyalpaaga, 'by nature', matches the idea that goodness comes out of what is already within.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; same idea of natural goodness, but the source is the heart, not the family line.

islam.quote_or_event: “Leave him as Haya' is a part of faith.”
islam.explanation: When a man scolded his brother for being too modest, the Prophet told him to stop, because modesty (haya') belongs to faith itself.
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat a sense of shame as a core part of a good character rather than a weakness.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong on shame, but ties it to faith rather than to lineage.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There are three distinguishing marks of this nation, the Jewish people. They are merciful, they are shamefaced, and they perform acts of kindness.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud has David name shame, mercy and kindness as the inherited marks of the descendants of Abraham, and says those who lack them are unfit to join the people.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats shamefacedness as a sign that belongs naturally to a good lineage.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 79a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; shame as a hereditary mark of a noble line is a close match.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, these two bright qualities guard the world. Which two? Conscience & concern.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names hiri and ottappa, shame at wrongdoing and fear of its results, as the pair that keeps the social order intact.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also pairs two qualities, rectitude and shame, and treats them as working together.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong match on the paired virtues, though the Buddha does not tie them to birth.

jainism.quote_or_event: Before Mahavira's birth, the god Sakra reflects that Arhats are never born into low, poor or mean families but only into noble lines such as the Ugras, Bhogas, Ikshvakus and Harivamsa, and so has the embryo moved to the womb of the Kshatriya queen Trisala.
jainism.explanation: The Kalpa Sutra's account of the embryo transfer shows that Jain narrative, like the Kural, could treat noble birth as a fitting vessel for exceptional virtue.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's claim that certain virtues appear naturally only in the well-born finds an echo in this Jain story about where great souls are born.
jainism.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira (Sakra's reflection and the embryo transfer), tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not re-verified this session; Jain doctrine elsewhere (e.g. Uttaradhyayana 12) insists birth has no spiritual value, so this narrative is only a partial parallel.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “You must be descended from a line of sceptre-bearing kings, for poor people do not have such sons as you are.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Menelaus, seeing Telemachus and Pisistratus at his table, guesses their royal lineage from their bearing before they say a word.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, Homer assumes that noble birth shows itself naturally in a person's manner.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; shares the Kural's belief that lineage shows in conduct, though shame and rectitude are not named.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “… they seem to have power to encourage and stimulate the generous-minded among our youth, and to make a character which is gently born, and a true lover of what is noble, ready to be possessed by virtue, they are not able to encourage the many to nobility and goodness. For these do not by nature obey the sense of shame, but only fear …”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says that moral arguments work only on a character that is already well-born and loves what is noble. The many, by nature, respond to fear of punishment rather than to a sense of shame.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Aristotle treats a natural responsiveness to shame as the mark of the well-born, something the many lack.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics X.9, 1179b (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Ross, Book X ch. 9). Strong match: shame as an inborn trait of the 'gently born' character. Aristotle's 'gently born' is about natural character more than family lineage, and he does not pair shame with rectitude as the Kural does.

kurals.tamil:
ஒழுக்கமும் வாய்மையும் நாணும்இம் மூன்றும்
இழுக்கார் குடிப்பிறந் தார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ozhukkamum vaaymaiyum naanum im moondrum
izhukkaar kudippirandhaar.
kurals.meaning: Those born into a good family never slip from these three: right conduct, truthfulness and a sense of shame.
kurals.elementary: Think of a three-legged stool: good behaviour, telling the truth, and feeling bad about doing wrong. If one leg breaks, the stool falls. Valluvar says people from a good family keep all three legs strong.
kurals.university: The couplet names a triad: ozhukkam (ஒழுக்கம், right conduct, the subject of chapter 14), vaaymai (வாய்மை, truthfulness, chapter 30) and naan (நாண், shame, which will receive its own chapter, 102). The verb izhukkaar (இழுக்கார்) means 'they do not slip or lapse', so the claim is about steadiness over a lifetime, not occasional virtue. Mu. Varadarasanar adds that the well-born live in the right path 'by nature' (இயல்பாகவே), linking this couplet to the iyalpaaga of 951, while Kalaignar again turns it into a definition: only those who never lapse in these three are to be counted high-born, and he glosses naan as maanam (மானம், honour). The word division நாணும்இம் மூன்றும் (naanum im moondrum, 'shame, these three') appears in both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the close of Vedic study the teacher charges the departing student: speak the truth, practise dharma, do not neglect study, and do not swerve from truth or from right conduct.
hinduism.explanation: The convocation address of the Taittiriya Upanishad joins truthful speech and righteous conduct as the lifelong duties of an educated householder.
hinduism.tie_back: Two of the Kural's three pillars, truth and conduct, are the heart of this charge.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; matches truth and conduct well, but shame is not named and lineage is not the frame.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Philippians to fix their minds on what is true, honest and pure.
christianity.tie_back: Truth and honest conduct, two of the Kural's three, sit at the head of Paul's list.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a general list of virtues rather than a triad tied to family.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with those who are true.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an joins God-consciousness with keeping company with the truthful.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural's insistence on truthfulness as a defining trait of the good.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; covers truthfulness only, so it is a next-best match.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel used to say: on three things does the world stand: On justice, on truth and on peace.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah names three supports on which the whole world rests.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it names a triad that must not be broken, with truth in the centre.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:18 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; parallel triad structure and shared stress on truth, but the other two members differ.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha says that one who has virtue and insight, who is principled, truthful and does his own duty is held dear by people.
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada joins moral conduct, truthfulness and diligence as the marks of a person others love.
buddhism.tie_back: Conduct and truth, two of the Kural's three, stand together here as well.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not re-verified verbatim this session; good on conduct and truth, silent on shame and lineage.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Doing no injury to living beings of the six orders, abstaining from lying and from taking what is not freely given, renouncing property, women, pride, and deceit, men should live under self-restraint.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Harikesa, born an outcast, tells proud Brahmins that true worth lies in non-injury, truthfulness and self-restraint.
jainism.tie_back: Right conduct and abstaining from lies, two of the Kural's three marks, are what Harikesa sets above birth.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; shares conduct and truth, but the Jain frame rejects the idea that birth guarantees them.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the embassy scene Achilles declares that he hates, as he hates the gates of Hades, the man who hides one thing in his heart and says another.
greek_mythology.explanation: The noblest of the Greek heroes defines himself by a refusal to say what he does not mean.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles shows the Kural's vaaymai, truthfulness, as part of a hero's nobility.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not re-verified this session; covers truthfulness only, and Achilles is far from a model of conduct in the same scene.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For the man who loves truth, and is truthful where nothing is at stake, will still more be truthful where something is at stake; he will avoid falsehood as something base, seeing that he avoided it even for its own sake; and such a man is worthy of praise.”
philosophy.explanation: Describing the truthful man as one who is true 'both in life and in word', Aristotle says his honesty is so fixed in his character that he shuns falsehood as shameful even when nothing depends on it.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's well-born, who never slip from truth, Aristotle's truthful man is steady in truth because lying is base to him.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.7, 1127b (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Ross, Book IV ch. 7). Partial match: it covers truthfulness and the sense that falsehood is base, but not the Kural's triad of conduct, truth and shame, nor its link to good birth.

kurals.tamil:
நகைஈகை இன்சொல் இகழாமை நான்கும்
வகையென்ப வாய்மைக் குடிக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Nagai eegai insol igazhaamai naangum
vagaiyenba vaaymaik kudikku.
kurals.meaning: A cheerful face, generosity, kind words and never belittling others: these four, the wise say, are the marks of a truly noble family.
kurals.elementary: When a friend visits, a kind family smiles, shares their snacks, speaks nicely and never makes fun of anyone. Valluvar says those four habits show you what a truly good family looks like.
kurals.university: The couplet lists four marks (naangum, நான்கும்): nagai (நகை, a smiling or cheerful countenance), eegai (ஈகை, giving, the subject of chapter 23), insol (இன்சொல், pleasant speech, chapter 10) and igazhaamai (இகழாமை, not scorning or belittling). Vaaymaik kudi (வாய்மைக் குடி) means a family that is genuinely, not nominally, noble; Puliyur Kesikan reads it as a lineage that never changes its character, and he applies the four marks especially to one's conduct towards the poor. Vagai (வகை) is 'kind' or 'proper quality', and enba (என்ப, 'they say') marks the list as received wisdom. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Manu tells the householder to say what is true and what is pleasing, not to speak an unpleasant truth nor a pleasant falsehood, and calls this the eternal law.
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu make pleasant, truthful speech a standing duty of the cultured householder.
hinduism.tie_back: It matches the Kural's insol, pleasant speech, as a mark of good breeding.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; covers only one of the four marks.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks the Corinthians to give freely and gladly rather than under pressure.
christianity.tie_back: The cheerful giver unites two of the Kural's marks, the smile and the gift.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a neat fit for nagai and eegai, silent on speech and scorn.

islam.quote_or_event: “Kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. And Allah is Free of need and Forbearing.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an ranks gentle words above a gift spoiled by insult or reminders of the favour.
islam.tie_back: It joins three of the Kural's four marks: giving, kind words, and not humiliating the recipient.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a close match on giving, kind speech and not belittling.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Shammai used to say: make your [study of the] Torah a fixed practice; speak little, but do much; and receive all men with a pleasant countenance.”
judaism.explanation: Shammai, famed for strictness, still teaches that every person should be greeted with a warm face.
judaism.tie_back: His 'pleasant countenance' is the Kural's nagai, the cheerful welcome.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:15 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong on the cheerful face, lighter on the other three marks.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches the young householder Sigala the four bases of sympathy that hold society together: generosity, kind speech, helpful conduct and impartial treatment of all.
buddhism.explanation: These four sangaha-vatthu are the Buddhist householder's tools for winning and keeping goodwill.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it gives a list of four social virtues, with generosity and kind speech in common.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a strikingly parallel set of four, though not tied to lineage.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Dasavaikalika teaches the monk purity of speech: he must not use harsh or hurtful words even when they are true, and must not call a one-eyed man one-eyed or a sick man sick, but speak in gentle, fitting terms.
jainism.explanation: Jain discipline treats wounding speech as a form of violence (himsa) and so forbids mocking or demeaning words.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's igazhaamai and insol, never belittling and always speaking kindly.
jainism.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra, ch. 7 (Vakyasuddhi, purity of speech)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from memory of the chapter's teaching, not verified against a live translation; covers speech only, not the smile or the gift.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the disguised Odysseus arrives as a ragged beggar, the swineherd Eumaeus welcomes him warmly, kills a pig for him and says it would not be right to slight any stranger, since strangers and beggars come from Zeus; later we learn Eumaeus was himself born a king's son.
greek_mythology.explanation: Eumaeus, a prince sold into slavery, keeps the gracious manners of his birth even as a servant.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His smile, gift, kind words and refusal to scorn the poor match all four of the Kural's marks of true nobility.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; an unusually full match, including the hidden royal birth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “How much better is it to join kind words to kind actions, and to enhance the value of our gifts by a civil and gracious commendation of them!”
philosophy.explanation: In this part of On Benefits, Seneca says the ready giver 'gives cheerfully and shows his disposition in his countenance' (II.2). He urges joining kind words to the gift (II.3) and warns that harsh words and a contemptuous manner make even kindnesses odious (II.4).
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca's good giver shows the Kural's four marks together: a cheerful face, generosity, kind words and no contempt for the one who receives.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Benefits (De Beneficiis) II.3, with II.2 and II.4 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Project Gutenberg (Stewart, eBook #3794, Book II chs. II-IV). Strong match on all four marks. Seneca, however, is describing how to give a benefit well, not the marks of a noble family.

kurals.tamil:
அடுக்கிய கோடி பெறினும் குடிப்பிறந்தார்
குன்றுவ செய்தல் இலர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Adukkiya kodi perinum kudippirandhaar
kundruva seydhal ilar.
kurals.meaning: Even if they could gain crores upon crores, the nobly born will not do anything that lowers their family's worth.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone offers you a giant pile of money if you will just cheat once. A person from a good family says no, because no pile of money is worth losing their good name.
kurals.university: Adukkiya kodi (அடுக்கிய கோடி) is 'crores stacked one upon another', hyperbole for limitless wealth, and perinum (பெறினும், 'even if they obtain') concedes the strongest temptation. Kundruva (குன்றுவ) are acts that diminish, literally 'that make small', and the commentators unanimously take the diminished thing to be the family's honour: Mu. Varadarasanar speaks of faults that would lower the family's distinction, and Kalaignar of deeds that would spoil that excellence. The couplet thus sets the chapter's characteristic contrast between wealth (Porul) and the inherited good name that the section on family (Kudiyiyal) values above it. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Harishchandra, tested by the sage Vishvamitra, gives away his whole kingdom, sells his wife and son and himself becomes a servant at a cremation ground rather than break his given word.
hinduism.explanation: The Puranic story makes Harishchandra the ideal of a king of the Solar line who will lose every possession before he loses his truth.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's well-born, he refuses any gain that would require a shameful act.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a well-known match, though the story turns on loss rather than refused gain.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Again, the devil taketh him up into an exceeding high mountain, and sheweth him all the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them; And saith unto him, All these things will I give thee, if thou wilt fall down and worship me. Then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan.”
christianity.explanation: Offered every kingdom on earth in exchange for one act of false worship, Jesus refuses outright.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's 'crores upon crores' offered and declined.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a dramatic match for refusing limitless gain, though the frame is fidelity to God rather than family honour.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not exchange the covenant of Allah for a small price. Indeed, what is with Allah is best for you, if only you could know.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an warns that any worldly price, however large it seems, is small next to keeping faith.
islam.tie_back: Both texts call any payment for a dishonourable act too low.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the same logic of refusing a price, without the lineage frame.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Yose ben Kisma tells how a man offered him a thousand thousand gold dinars, precious stones and pearls to come and live in his town, and he replied that even for all the silver and gold in the world he would live only in a place of Torah.
judaism.explanation: The sage turns down a fortune rather than leave the setting that keeps him true to his calling.
judaism.tie_back: His 'thousand thousand' dinars echo the Kural's piled-up crores, refused for something worth more.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from the Hebrew text checked on Sefaria; a close match on refusing vast wealth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He is indeed virtuous, wise, and righteous who neither for his own sake nor for the sake of another (does any wrong), who does not crave for sons, wealth, or kingdom, and does not desire success by unjust means.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada defines the righteous person as one who will not seek wealth or power by wrong means.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sets wealth gained through wrongdoing below the person's integrity.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near match, minus the family frame.

jainism.quote_or_event: When Indra, in disguise, urges King Nami to increase his gold, silver and treasure before renouncing, Nami answers that even countless mountains of gold and silver as large as Kailasa would not satisfy a greedy man, for desire is as endless as the sky.
jainism.explanation: The royal sage Nami refuses to let any amount of treasure turn him from his chosen path.
jainism.tie_back: His mountains of gold are the Jain counterpart to the Kural's piled crores, and both are refused.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 9 (The Pravrajya of King Nami), tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not re-verified this session; the theme is renunciation of greed rather than protecting family honour.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Prodicus's fable, the young Heracles at a crossroads is met by Vice, who promises him every pleasure without toil, and by Virtue, who promises honour through hard work, and he chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: The hero turns down an easy life of luxury for the harder road that keeps his honour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's well-born, Heracles will not trade his worth for easy gain.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a general choice of virtue over pleasure rather than a refusal of a specific bribe.

philosophy.quote_or_event: At his trial Socrates tells the jury that he will not stop doing philosophy even to be acquitted, and that virtue does not come from money, but money and every other good come from virtue.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates refuses to buy his life by abandoning what he thinks right.
philosophy.tie_back: He shows the Kural's resolve: no gain, even life itself, is worth a deed that lowers one's worth.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; strong on refusing advantage for principle, silent on lineage.

kurals.tamil:
வழங்குவ துள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும் பழங்குடி
பண்பில் தலைப்பிரிதல் இன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Vazhanguvadhu ulveezhndhak kannum pazhangudi
panbil thalaippiridhal indru.
kurals.meaning: Even when their means for giving have shrunk, those of an old and worthy family never part from their generous character.
kurals.elementary: A grandmother who used to cook big meals for everyone now has only a little rice, but she still shares it with a hungry neighbour. Valluvar says that is how people from a good old family act: they keep giving even when they have little.
kurals.university: Vazhanguvadhu (வழங்குவது) is 'that which is given', and ulveezhndha (உள்வீழ்ந்த) means 'fallen inward, shrunk', so the opening line pictures the family's power of giving contracting through poverty; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as the capacity to give having dwindled through want. Pazhangudi (பழங்குடி) is 'the ancient family', the old line whose character is long established, and thalaippiridhal (தலைப்பிரிதல்) means 'to separate from', here from their panbu (பண்பு, nature, especially the generous disposition). Sivayogi Sivakumar and Solomon Pappaiah both specify that it is the giving nature that endures, while Kalaignar explicitly names poverty as the blow. Both sites print the words as வழங்குவ துள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும், a traditional metrical division of வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Rantideva, of the Lunar line, gives away all his wealth and then, after forty-eight days without food or water, gives the little food and water that finally reach him to a Brahmin, a Shudra, a man with dogs and an outcast who come begging, keeping nothing for himself.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana presents Rantideva as a king who kept giving even after his wealth was gone and he himself was starving.
hinduism.tie_back: He is the Kural's pazhangudi in person: a royal line's generosity that survives total poverty.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a near one-to-one match, including the royal lineage.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Verily I say unto you, That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury: For all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus praises a poor widow who gave her last coins, valuing her gift above the large gifts of the rich.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it honours generosity that continues when the means have shrunk to almost nothing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong match on giving from want, though the widow's lineage is not the point.

islam.quote_or_event: “They love those who emigrated to them and find not any want in their breasts of what the emigrants were given but give [them] preference over themselves, even though they are in privation.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an praises the Ansar of Medina, who shared with the refugees from Mecca even when they themselves were in need.
islam.tie_back: Giving others preference 'even though they are in privation' is exactly the Kural's generosity that survives poverty.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match on giving in privation.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud tells that Hillel, when a man from a good family fell into poverty, provided him with a horse to ride and a servant to run before him, to keep him in the manner to which he had been accustomed.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis teach that the dignity of a once-prosperous family should be preserved even when its wealth is gone.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts insist that a good family's character and standing outlast the loss of its wealth.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not re-verified this session; the angle is reversed, since here others preserve the fallen family's dignity rather than the family continuing to give.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sasa Jataka, the Bodhisatta is born as a hare who has no rice or meat to offer a begging Brahmin on a fast day, so he leaps into the fire to offer his own body as food.
buddhism.explanation: Having nothing else to give, the hare gives himself, and Sakka marks the moon with his image in honour of the gift.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's ancient family, the hare does not stop giving just because his means have run out.
buddhism.source: Sasa Jataka (No. 316), The Jataka vol. III, ed. E. B. Cowell
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a strong match for giving when one has nothing, though no lineage theme.

jainism.quote_or_event: Chandana, a princess of the royal house of Champa, is sold into slavery after her city falls, chained and given only boiled lentils in a winnowing basket; when Mahavira comes begging after a long fast she gladly offers him that meagre food, and the gift completes his vow.
jainism.explanation: In Jain tradition Chandanbala keeps the generous heart of her royal birth even as a bound and starving slave, and later becomes the head of Mahavira's order of nuns.
jainism.tie_back: She is the Kural's pazhangudi in Jain form: noble character that does not leave her even when she has almost nothing to give.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacaritra, Book 10 (Mahaviracaritra), tr. Helen M. Johnson
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not re-verified this session; a strong narrative match, with royal lineage, ruin and continued giving all present.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, a poor old couple, are the only people in their region to welcome Jupiter and Mercury in disguise, offering what little they have with cheerful hearts and even trying to kill their only goose for the guests.
greek_mythology.explanation: Their humble hospitality is rewarded when the gods turn their hut into a temple.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's old family, they keep giving gladly despite having almost nothing.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; strong on giving in poverty, though the couple are not of a noble line.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says liberality is judged relative to a person's means, so a man who gives less may be the more liberal if he gives from smaller resources, and he notes that liberal people rarely grow rich because they do not hoard.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle generosity is a settled disposition, not a matter of the size of the gift.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's point is the same: the generous character remains even when the amount one can give shrinks.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.1 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a close philosophical statement of the Kural's claim.

kurals.tamil:
சலம்பற்றிச் சால்பில செய்யார்மா சற்ற
குலம்பற்றி வாழ்தும்என் பார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Salampatrich chaalbila seyyaar maasatra
kulampatri vaazhdhum enbaar.
kurals.meaning: Those who resolve to live true to their spotless family line will never stoop to deceit or do anything unworthy.
kurals.elementary: If your family has always been known for honesty, you think, 'I will not be the one who spoils our name.' So you do not cheat, even when it would be easy.
kurals.university: Salam (சலம்) means deceit or crookedness, which Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar render as vanchanai (வஞ்சனை); chaalbila (சால்பில) are acts lacking saalbu (சால்பு, worthiness, nobility of character, the subject of chapter 99). Maasatra kulam (மாசற்ற குலம்) is 'a family free of stain', and vaazhdhum enbaar (வாழ்தும் என்பார்) are 'those who say, we shall live (by it)', so the couplet describes a conscious resolve to keep faith with an unblemished line. Solomon Pappaiah adds 'even when poverty comes', reading the couplet as continuing the thought of 955 that hardship tests the well-born. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net, both dividing the line as மா சற்ற / மாசற்ற across the metrical break.

hinduism.quote_or_event: On the battlefield Arjuna fears that destroying families will destroy the ancient family traditions (kula-dharma), and that when these perish the whole family is overcome by lawlessness.
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna treats the inherited duties of a family line as something precious that wrong action can wipe out.
hinduism.tie_back: He shares the Kural's concern to keep a family's tradition unstained, though Krishna goes on to overrule his conclusion.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; shares the value placed on family tradition, but it is Arjuna's argument that the Gita then answers, so it is a next-best match.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says his company has given up every hidden dishonesty and crafty dealing.
christianity.tie_back: Its refusal of 'craftiness' is the Kural's refusal of salam, deceit.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong on deceit, but the motive is faithfulness to the gospel, not to a family name.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not mix the truth with falsehood or conceal the truth while you know [it].”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an forbids deceit that blends truth and falsehood.
islam.tie_back: It forbids the salam, crookedness, that the Kural's well-born refuse.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; addresses deceit only, without the lineage motive, so a next-best match.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs says that a righteous man who walks in his integrity leaves his children blessed after him.
judaism.explanation: The integrity of one generation becomes the inheritance of the next.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties personal honesty to the good name of the family line.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not re-verified this session; links integrity and lineage, but from parent to child rather than child to ancestors.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whosoever is given to anger, is miserly, has base desires, and is selfish, deceitful, shameless and fearless (in doing evil) — know him as an outcast.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that deceit and shamelessness, not birth, are what make a person low.
buddhism.tie_back: It agrees with the Kural that deceit is unworthy of anyone claiming a good name, though it denies that birth gives that name.
buddhism.source: Vasala Sutta, Sn 1.7, v. 18 (tr. Piyadassi Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; same condemnation of deceit, with an anti-hereditary frame.

jainism.quote_or_event: “I am the daughter of the Bhôga-king, and you are an Andhakavrishni; being born in a noble family let us not become like Gandhana-snakes; firmly practise self-control!”
jainism.explanation: When the monk Rathanemi tries to seduce the nun Rajimati in a cave, she reminds him of their noble houses and calls him back to his vows, and he returns to the Law.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural's resolve exactly: because we live by a spotless lineage, we will not do anything unworthy.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified); a near one-to-one match, and the verse says she 'maintained the honour of her clan and family'.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Glaucus tells Diomedes that his father Hippolochus sent him to Troy urging him always to be the best and not to bring shame on the race of his fathers, who were the noblest in Ephyra and Lycia.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Lycian hero's whole code of conduct is framed as loyalty to an ancestral line.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's well-born, Glaucus acts as he does because he will not stain his family's name.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not re-verified this session; a close match on lineage as a motive for conduct.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Count it the greatest of all sins to prefer life to honour, and to lose, for the sake of living, all that makes life worth having.”
philosophy.explanation: Writing to a young noble, Juvenal says that no pressure, not even a tyrant's threat, should make him trade honour for survival.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's well-born refuse unworthy acts for the same reason: honour is what makes their life worth having.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (capitalisation adjusted); Satire 8 is addressed to a man of noble pedigree, making the fit strong.

kurals.tamil:
குடிப்பிறந்தார் கண்விளங்கும் குற்றம் விசும்பின்
மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல் உயர்ந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Kudippirandhaar kan vilangum kutram visumbin
madhikkan maruppol uyarndhu.
kurals.meaning: A fault in someone of good birth stands out for all to see, like the dark spot on the moon high in the sky.
kurals.elementary: A tiny ink spot on a dirty shirt is hard to see, but the same spot on a bright white shirt is easy to notice. Valluvar says that a small mistake by someone from a respected family shows up just like that spot.
kurals.university: The simile is visumbin madhikkan maru (விசும்பின் மதிக்கண் மறு), 'the blemish on the moon in the sky'; maru (மறு) is a spot or stain, which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses as kalangam (களங்கம்). Uyarndhu (உயர்ந்து, 'being high, raised up') does double work: the moon is high in the sky, and the well-born are high in society, so their flaws are exposed to everyone. Puliyur Kesikan adds that the fault may be small in size yet known to the whole world, and Kalaignar notes that it shows 'without any concealment'. Sivayogi Sivakumar's gloss reads the image as the full moon itself, but the standard commentators understand the dark mark on its face. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna says that whatever a great person does, ordinary people follow, and whatever standard he sets, the world pursues.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita warns that the conduct of the eminent is watched and copied by everyone.
hinduism.tie_back: Because the great are watched, as the Kural says, their faults cannot hide.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; shares the visibility of the eminent, though the Gita stresses imitation more than exposure.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples that, set on high, their lives will be seen by all.
christianity.tie_back: Like the moon in the Kural, a city on a hill cannot conceal what is on it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong image of high visibility, though aimed at good works rather than faults.

islam.quote_or_event: “O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you should commit a clear immorality - for her the punishment would be doubled two fold, and ever is that, for Allah, easy.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an holds those in the Prophet's household to a higher standard, so a fault in them weighs double.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says that high station magnifies a fault.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a good match on status magnifying wrongdoing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Woe to so-and-so who studied Torah, woe to his father who taught him Torah, woe to his teacher who taught him Torah.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud says that when a learned person is dishonest in business or rude to others, people blame not only him but his father and teacher, and so God's name is desecrated.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the fault of someone from an honoured line is seen by all and shames the line itself.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 86a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a close match, with the shame spreading to the father as the Kural implies.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada says that one who covers the evil he has done with good deeds lights up the world like the moon freed from clouds.
buddhism.explanation: The verse uses the moon as an image of a life made bright again after wrongdoing.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts use the moon to show how clearly a person's conduct is seen, though the Dhammapada looks to redemption rather than exposure.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not re-verified this session; shares the moon image but makes a different point.

jainism.quote_or_event: After defeating his brother Bharata, the prince Bahubali renounces the world and stands motionless in meditation for a year, but omniscience will not come because of one small fault, his pride at not wanting to bow to his younger brothers who became monks before him; his sisters Brahmi and Sundari tell him to come down from the elephant of pride, and when he lets it go he becomes omniscient.
jainism.explanation: In Jain narrative even a tiny flaw in so great a soul stands out and holds him back.
jainism.tie_back: Like the moon's spot in the Kural, Bahubali's one small fault is conspicuous precisely because everything else about him is so great.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacaritra, Book 1 (Bharata and Bahubali), tr. Helen M. Johnson
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not re-verified this session; a good picture of a small flaw in a great person, but the emphasis is spiritual hindrance rather than public visibility.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Tantalus, a son of Zeus who dined with the gods, abuses that honour by stealing their nectar and ambrosia, and his crime is punished forever and brings a curse on his descendants, the house of Atreus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pindar says Tantalus could not digest his great good fortune, and his fall is all the more famous because of how high he stood.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's well-born, Tantalus's fault is magnified by his high birth and stains his whole line.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a real myth of a high-born fault, but it is a grave crime, not a small spot made visible.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Then the nobility of your own parents begins to rise up in judgment against you, and to hold a glaring torch over your misdeeds. The greater the sinner's name, the more signal the guiltiness of the sin.”
philosophy.explanation: Juvenal tells a young aristocrat that his famous ancestry does not excuse his vices but lights them up for all to see.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's moon-spot in Roman form: noble birth shines a light on every fault.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match, down to the image of light exposing the fault.

kurals.tamil:
நலத்தின்கண் நாரின்மை தோன்றின் அவனைக்
குலத்தின்கண் ஐயப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nalaththinkan naarinmai thondrin avanaik
kulaththinkan aiyap padum.
kurals.meaning: If a lack of love shows up in someone who seems good, people will begin to doubt that he really comes from the family he claims.
kurals.elementary: If a boy from a famously kind family is mean to a puppy, people say, 'Is he really from that kind family?' Valluvar says that being unkind makes others wonder where you came from.
kurals.university: Naar (நார்) is literally 'fibre', the tough strand that binds, and by extension affection or love; naarinmai (நாரின்மை) is the want of it, which Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan gloss as anbu-inmai or arul-inmai, lack of love or compassion. The opening word nalam (நலம்) is read in several ways: Mu. Varadarasanar takes it as one's good qualities, Puliyur Kesikan as the family's distinction, and Kalaignar as beauty and renown. Aiyap padum (ஐயப் படும், 'will be doubted') makes the striking claim that conduct can call ancestry itself into question, which is the hinge between this chapter's praise of lineage and the ethical reading that says character, not birth, is the real proof. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the serpent Nahusha asks Yudhishthira who is a true Brahmin, Yudhishthira answers that it is the one in whom truth, charity, forgiveness, good conduct, gentleness, austerity and compassion are seen, and that a Shudra with these marks is no Shudra and a Brahmin without them is no Brahmin.
hinduism.explanation: In the Mahabharata Yudhishthira argues that conduct, not birth, is what proves a person's standing.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, he says that a lack of compassion casts doubt on any claim of high birth.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Ajagara Parva, Nahusha's questions), tr. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a strong match on character testing birth, though the frame is varna rather than family.

christianity.quote_or_event: “They answered and said unto him, Abraham is our father. Jesus saith unto them, If ye were Abraham's children, ye would do the works of Abraham.”
christianity.explanation: When his opponents boast of descent from Abraham, Jesus answers that their actions call that descent into question.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's logic exactly: unworthy conduct makes people doubt the lineage claimed.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match on conduct disproving a lineage claim.

islam.quote_or_event: “O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says tribes and lineages exist only so people can know one another, and that true nobility is righteousness.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes character, not pedigree, the real test of a person's worth.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong on character over lineage, though it does not single out love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Anyone who has compassion for God's creatures, it is known that he is of the descendants of Abraham, our father, and anyone who does not have compassion for God's creatures, it is known that he is not of the descendants of Abraham, our father.”
judaism.explanation: When rich Babylonian Jews refused to help a visitor, a sage declared that their lack of compassion proved they did not truly descend from Abraham.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost word for word the Kural: lack of love makes one's lineage doubtful.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Beitzah 32b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a near one-to-one match on compassion as proof of lineage.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whosoever in this world kills living beings, once born or twice born, in whom there is no sympathy for living beings — know him as an outcast.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells a proud Brahmin that a lack of sympathy for living things, not birth, is what makes someone an outcast.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says that the absence of love reveals what a person really is, whatever their birth.
buddhism.source: Vasala Sutta, Sn 1.7, v. 2 (tr. Piyadassi Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong match on lack of compassion defining one's real standing.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Those who are full of anger and pride, who kill, lie, steal, and own property, are Brâhmanas without pure birth and knowledge; they are very bad fields.”
jainism.explanation: When Brahmins proud of their pure birth mock and beat the outcast-born monk Harikesa, the protecting Yaksha declares that their cruelty shows they lack the very birth they boast of.
jainism.tie_back: Their lack of kindness, as in the Kural, makes their claimed lineage doubtful, and the lecture ends by saying birth appears of no value beside virtue.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified); a close match on cruelty disproving high birth.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Athena, disguised as Mentor, tells Telemachus that few sons are as good as their fathers, most are worse and only a few better, but that he has shown he has his father's spirit.
greek_mythology.explanation: The goddess treats a son's conduct as the test of whether he truly carries his father's line.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it implies that a son who lacks his family's qualities makes people doubt the connection.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not re-verified this session; good on conduct testing lineage, but love is not the specific quality.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca writes that a hall full of smoke-darkened ancestral portraits does not make a man noble, that the soul alone makes one well-born, and that the well-born man is the one fitted by nature for virtue.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca moves nobility from family records to character.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he implies that a man who lacks virtue has no real claim to his pedigree.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters 44 (tr. R. M. Gummere)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not re-verified this session; strong on virtue as true nobility, not specific to lack of love.

kurals.tamil:
நிலத்தில் கிடந்தமை கால்காட்டும் காட்டும்
குலத்தில் பிறந்தார்வாய்ச் சொல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nilaththil kidandhamai kaal kaattum kaattum
kulaththil pirandhaarvaaich chol.
kurals.meaning: Just as a sprout shows the nature of the soil it grew in, a person's words show the family they come from.
kurals.elementary: A healthy green plant tells you the soil is good. In the same way, when someone speaks kindly and wisely, you can tell they grew up in a good home.
kurals.university: The image is agricultural: kaal (கால்) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan as mulai (முளை), the sprout or shoot, which reveals (kaattum, காட்டும்) what lay hidden in the soil (nilaththil kidandhamai, நிலத்தில் கிடந்தமை). Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar widen it to the crop that grows there. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads kaal in its common sense of 'foot', so that the soil clinging to one's feet shows where one has walked; this is a minority reading that the standard commentators do not follow. The repetition kaattum kaattum (காட்டும் காட்டும்) closes the simile and opens its application: so too the speech (vaaich chol, வாய்ச்சொல்) of those born in a family reveals that family. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the boy Satyakama asks to become a pupil, he honestly tells the sage Gautama that he does not know his father's name or his lineage, since his mother does not know it either; Gautama replies that no one but a Brahmin could speak so truthfully, and accepts him.
hinduism.explanation: In the Chandogya Upanishad, the boy's truthful words reveal his worth when no family record can.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim in story form: a person's speech shows the lineage behind them.
hinduism.source: Chandogya Upanishad 4.4 (tr. F. Max Müller, SBE 1)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a near one-to-one match on speech revealing lineage, though here it reveals worth rather than confirming a known family.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Either make the tree good, and his fruit good; or else make the tree corrupt, and his fruit corrupt: for the tree is known by his fruit. O generation of vipers, how can ye, being evil, speak good things? for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says a tree is known by what it produces, and a person by the words that come from the heart.
christianity.tie_back: The same two steps as the Kural: what grows shows the source, and speech shows the person.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near match on both the plant image and speech as revelation.

islam.quote_or_event: “Have you not considered how Allah presents an example, [making] a good word like a good tree, whose root is firmly fixed and its branches [high] in the sky?”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an compares a good word to a good tree, rooted firmly and reaching high.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it joins speech and plant growth, with roots below and fruit above.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong shared image of speech as plant, though lineage is not mentioned.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When two people quarrel with each other, they observe which of them becomes silent first. Then they say: This silent party is of finer lineage.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud reports that in the Land of Israel people tested a family's lineage by how its members spoke in a quarrel.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the rabbis read a person's ancestry from the way they use their mouth.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 71b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a close match, with restrained speech as the sign of good lineage.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha says a person's discernment can be known through discussion, if one pays attention over a long time, just as integrity is known by living together and purity by dealings.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta teaches that a person's inner quality is revealed in how they speak and reason.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats speech as the outward shoot that shows the inner soil.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not re-verified this session; speech reveals character, not lineage.

jainism.quote_or_event: The monk Jayaghosha tells the priest Vijayaghosha that one does not become a Brahmana by uttering the sacred syllable om nor a Sramana by being tonsured, but by one's actions one becomes a Brahmana, a Kshatriya, a Vaisya or a Sudra.
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana says that outward signs, including ritual words, do not prove one's class; conduct does.
jainism.tie_back: It agrees with the Kural that what comes out of a person reveals what they are, but it denies that ritual speech alone proves birth.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 25 (The True Sacrifice), tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not re-verified this session; a next-best match, since the Jain text stresses deeds over words and rejects birth-based class.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “It is plain you take after your father. One can soon see when a man is son to one whom heaven has blessed both as regards wife and offspring.”
greek_mythology.explanation: After young Pisistratus speaks with tact at the dinner table, Menelaus recognises Nestor's wisdom in his words.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim in Homer: a young man's speech shows the family he comes from.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match, as Menelaus reads lineage from speech, and later tells Telemachus that what he says 'shows that you come of good family'.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca quotes a Greek proverb that a man's speech is just like his life, and argues that the style of a person's words reflects the state of their character.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, the way someone speaks is an index of their inner life.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's sprout, speech shows what lies beneath.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters 114 (tr. R. M. Gummere)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not re-verified this session; strong on speech revealing character, silent on lineage.

kurals.tamil:
நலம்வேண்டின் நாணுடைமை வேண்டும் குலம்வேண்டின்
வேண்டுக யார்க்கும் பணிவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Nalamvendin naanudaimai vendum kulamvendin
venduga yaarkkum panivu.
kurals.meaning: If you want goodness, you must have a sense of shame; if you want a noble family name, you must be humble towards everyone.
kurals.elementary: Kids who say 'I'm the best!' all the time do not get respect. Kids who are polite to everyone, even the youngest, do. Valluvar says that if you want your family to be respected, be humble with everyone.
kurals.university: The closing couplet turns the chapter from description to instruction with a double condition built on the verb vendu (வேண்டு, 'to want, to require'): nalam vendin (நலம் வேண்டின், 'if you want good') requires naanudaimai (நாணுடைமை, the possession of shame), and kulam vendin (குலம் வேண்டின், 'if you want family standing') requires panivu (பணிவு, humility) towards yaarkkum (யார்க்கும், everyone). Puliyur Kesikan specifies shame at blame (பழிக்கு நாணம்), and Kalaignar adds 'without arrogance' (ஆணவமின்றி). The effect is to make lineage something earned and maintained by humility rather than simply inherited, which ties the chapter's ending back to the 'by nature' of 951. Naanudaimai is also the title of chapter 102, and the two chapters are often read together. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna begins his list of the marks of true knowledge with humility (amanitvam) and freedom from pride (adambhitvam), followed by non-violence, patience and simplicity.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita places humility first among the qualities of the wise.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes humility the foundation of real standing.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; strong on humility, though the Gita ties it to knowledge rather than family name.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that honour comes to those who humble themselves, not to those who seek it.
christianity.tie_back: This matches the Kural's paradox: humility is the way to a noble name.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a close match on humility as the path to honour.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth easily, and when the ignorant address them [harshly], they say [words of] peace.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an describes God's true servants as walking humbly and answering rudeness with peace.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes humility towards everyone, even the rude, the mark of the honoured.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong on humility towards all, silent on lineage.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Meir said: Engage but little in business, and busy yourself with the Torah. Be of humble spirit before all men.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Meir tells his students to be humble before every person.
judaism.tie_back: 'Before all men' is the Kural's yaarkkum panivu, humility towards everyone.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:10 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near match on humility towards all.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To be respectful, humble, contented and grateful; and to listen to the Dhamma on due occasions — this is the greatest blessing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Mangala Sutta counts humility among the highest blessings of life.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes humility a source of good fortune and standing.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; good on humility, not tied to family name.

jainism.quote_or_event: “'Frequently (I have been born) in a high family, frequently in a low one; I am not mean, nor noble, nor do I desire (social preferment).' Thus reflecting, who would brag about his family or about his glory, or for what should he long?”
jainism.explanation: Because the soul has been born countless times in high and low families, the Acaranga says no one has grounds to be proud of their family; Jain doctrine also teaches that pride and self-praise bind karma that leads to low birth, while humility leads to high birth.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes humility, not boasting, the right attitude to family standing, though for Jainism high birth is itself the fruit of humility.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra I.2.3.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the karma point (Tattvartha Sutra 6.25-26 on gotra karma) is paraphrased in the explanation, not quoted.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, boasts to the women of Thebes about her divine ancestry and her fourteen children and says she deserves worship more than the goddess Leto; Apollo and Artemis kill her children and she is turned to weeping stone.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid tells the story as the destruction of a proud family through boasting.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Niobe shows the reverse of the Kural's advice: pride in lineage ruins the lineage.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a strong cautionary match, framed negatively.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Laws, Plato's Athenian says that justice always follows God, and whoever would be happy holds fast to her and follows in her company with humility and order, while one who is lifted up with pride of wealth, rank or beauty is soon left alone and brings ruin on himself and his house.
philosophy.explanation: Plato ties lasting good fortune to humility and warns that pride ruins both the person and his household.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he makes humility the condition for a person's and a family's good standing.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not re-verified this session; a close thematic match that even mentions the ruin of one's house.
